2284: Part of the Writings in the Hebrew Bible. The Septuagint arranges the later collections in a different order and has many additional lines. The deuterocanonical *Wisdom of Ben Sira* (Sirach, or Ecclesiasticus), written in Hebrew around 180 BC and translated into Greek by the author's grandson, continues the tradition of Proverbs; it is canonical in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles and among the Apocrypha in Protestant ones.
2286: Wisdom literature (reflective monologue framed by an editor)
2287: Solomon, identified with 'the Preacher (Qohelet), the son of David, king in Jerusalem' (Eccl 1:1; Eccl 1:12). The Talmud says Hezekiah and his company wrote it down (Baba Bathra 15a).
2288: Most scholars, including many conservatives (Franz Delitzsch in the 19th century famously among them), regard the Solomonic persona as a literary device. The Hebrew is late, with features close to Mishnaic Hebrew, Aramaic influence and probable Persian loanwords such as *pardes* ('park', Eccl 2:5) and *pitgam* ('sentence', Eccl 8:11). A frame narrator speaks of Qohelet in the third person (Eccl 1:2; Eccl 12:9-14). Dates usually proposed range from the Persian period to the 3rd century BC.
2290: Thoughtful people confronted with injustice, death and the apparent meaninglessness of human striving, especially the educated and comfortable.
2291: Jerusalem, in the voice of a king who has tested every source of meaning 'under the sun'.
2292: To expose the vanity (Hebrew *hevel*, 'vapour, breath') of seeking lasting gain from wisdom, pleasure, work or wealth, and to commend receiving life as God's gift with joy and reverence, fearing God and keeping his commandments.
2294: The limits of wisdom and the certainty of death
2295: Joy in ordinary life as God's gift
2297: Fear God and keep his commandments
2299: The king's experiment with wisdom, pleasure and toil
2300: A time for everything; injustice and the limits of human life
2301: Counsels for living wisely in an uncertain world
2302: Epilogue: the end of the matter
2303: Ecclesiastes faces honestly the world under the curse of Gen 3, where toil is frustrating and death levels everyone. Paul's statement that creation was 'subjected to futility' in hope of liberation (Rom 8:20-21) uses the same Greek word the Septuagint uses for Ecclesiastes' 'vanity', and Christians have read the book as clearing the ground for the hope of resurrection.
2304: Hebrew title *Qohelet*; in the Writings among the five Megillot and read at Sukkot (Tabernacles). The Mishnah (Yadayim 3:5) records rabbinic debate over whether it 'defiles the hands', that is, whether it is sacred Scripture; the view that it does prevailed.
2307: Solomon, from the title 'The song of songs, which is Solomon's' (Song 1:1); the Talmud credits Hezekiah and his company with writing it down (Baba Bathra 15a).
2308: Many scholars read the Hebrew *lishlomoh* as 'for' or 'concerning' Solomon rather than 'by' him, and see the Song as an anthology or unified cycle of love poems by an unknown poet. Its language includes possible Persian and Greek loanwords (e.g. *pardes*, Song 4:13; *appiryon*, 'palanquin', Song 3:9), suggesting a post-exilic date, though some argue older poetry was later updated. It has clear parallels with Egyptian love songs of the New Kingdom period.
2309: Read at face value, young lovers and the community celebrating marriage; read allegorically, Israel or the church in relationship with God.
2310: Rural and royal scenes in Israel: vineyards, gardens, Lebanon, Jerusalem and Solomon's court.
2311: Interpretations differ. Literal readings see a celebration of exclusive, faithful, sensual love between a man and a woman as a good gift of the Creator. Allegorical readings (the Targum and much rabbinic tradition: God and Israel; Origen, Bernard of Clairvaux and much Christian tradition: Christ and the church or the soul) see the love of God for his people. Some read it as a drama with two main characters, others with three (the 'shepherd hypothesis', in which the woman resists Solomon for her shepherd lover).
2312: The goodness of human love and desire
2315: Do not awaken love before its time
2320: Wedding procession and union in the garden
2323: The Song restores a picture of love like that of Eden before shame (Gen 2:25), affirming bodily love within God's good creation. Because Scripture often pictures God's covenant as a marriage (Hos 2; Eph 5:31-32; Rev 19:7), Jewish and Christian readers have also heard in it the love that God has for his people.
2324: Part of the Five Megillot in the Hebrew Bible and read at Passover. The Mishnah (Yadayim 3:5) records Rabbi Akiva defending it as the 'holy of holies' among the Writings. In Catholic and Orthodox Bibles it is followed by the deuterocanonical *Wisdom of Solomon*, a Greek work probably from Alexandria (1st c. BC), written in Solomon's voice, on wisdom, immortality and God's judgment; Protestant Bibles that print it place it among the Apocrypha. (Sirach is noted under Proverbs.)
2327: Isaiah son of Amoz, who prophesied in Jerusalem under Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah (Isa 1:1), roughly 740–681 BC, writing the whole book including the predictions of Cyrus by name (Isa 44:28; Isa 45:1). Defenders of unity note shared vocabulary across the book (e.g. 'the Holy One of Israel'), the single Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran, and New Testament citations from both halves under Isaiah's name (John 12:38-41).
2328: Most critical scholars distinguish First Isaiah (Isa 1-39, largely 8th century, with later additions such as Isa 24-27 and Isa 34-35), Second or Deutero-Isaiah (Isa 40-55, an anonymous prophet in Babylonian exile c. 550–539 BC, who addresses Cyrus as a contemporary), and Third or Trito-Isaiah (Isa 56-66, from the restored community in Judah after 539 BC). This three-part view goes back to Bernhard Duhm (1892), building on earlier work. Recent scholarship emphasises the book's deliberate unity as a whole, often speaking of an 'Isaianic school' that preserved and extended the prophet's message.
2331: Judah and Jerusalem facing the Assyrian threat (Isa 1-39); exiles in Babylon awaiting release (Isa 40-55); and the returned community struggling to rebuild (Isa 56-66).
2332: Jerusalem in the age of Assyrian expansion (the Syro-Ephraimite crisis of 734 BC, the fall of Samaria in 722 BC and Sennacherib's siege in 701 BC), then the horizon of Babylonian exile and the rise of Cyrus of Persia.
2333: To call Judah to trust the Holy One of Israel rather than foreign alliances, to announce judgment and a purified remnant, and to proclaim comfort, a new exodus, the redemptive work of the Servant of the LORD, and a renewed creation in which the nations stream to Zion.
2336: The coming royal son of David
2337: The Servant of the LORD who suffers for many
2339: New heavens and new earth; the nations come to Zion
2346: The 'Isaiah Apocalypse': world judgment and feast
2347: Woes, trust and the coming restoration
2351: The LORD versus idols; Cyrus his anointed
2354: The restored community and the new creation
2357: Isaiah spans the whole arc of Israel's story from sin and judgment to exile and a new creation, which is why it is sometimes called 'the fifth gospel'. Jesus begins his ministry by reading Isa 61 (Luke 4:16-21), and the New Testament repeatedly identifies him as the Immanuel child, the Davidic shoot and the Servant who bore the sins of many (Acts 8:32-35).
2358: First of the Latter Prophets in the Hebrew Bible (though the Talmud, Baba Bathra 14b, lists Jeremiah and Ezekiel before it). The Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a) from Qumran, copied around the 2nd century BC, is the oldest complete manuscript of any biblical book and agrees substantially with the later Masoretic text.
2360: Prophecy (poetic oracles, prose sermons and biographical narrative)
2361: Jeremiah son of Hilkiah, a priest from Anathoth, who dictated his oracles to his scribe Baruch (Jer 36:4; Jer 36:32). The Talmud credits Jeremiah with his own book, Kings and Lamentations (Baba Bathra 15a).
2362: Scholars since Bernhard Duhm and Sigmund Mowinckel have distinguished poetic oracles (often attributed to Jeremiah himself), biographical prose about him (often linked to Baruch), and prose sermons in Deuteronomistic style (attributed by many to later editors). Views range from substantial Jeremianic authorship with Baruch's help to extensive exilic and post-exilic editing. The existence of a shorter Greek edition shows the book grew in stages.
2363: Start of Jeremiah's ministry (13th year of Josiah)
2365: Judah and Jerusalem in their last decades before the Babylonian conquest, and the exiles in Babylon and refugees in Egypt afterward.
2366: From the 13th year of Josiah (627 BC) through the reigns of Jehoiakim and Zedekiah to the fall of Jerusalem (586 BC) and the flight to Egypt.
2367: To call Judah to repent, to announce that judgment through Babylon was certain because of covenant breaking, to expose false prophets and false trust in the temple, and to promise restoration after seventy years and a new covenant written on the heart.
2369: False security in the temple and false prophets
2371: Submission to Babylon as God's will for the time
2378: Kings, false prophets and seventy years
2379: Conflicts with priests, prophets and kings; letter to exiles
2380: Book of Consolation: the new covenant
2381: The final years and the fall
2383: Imprisonment and the fall of Jerusalem
2385: Historical appendix: the fall of Jerusalem
2386: Jeremiah witnesses the end of the old order of king, temple and land, but promises a new covenant in which God will forgive sin and write his law on hearts. Jesus speaks of 'the new covenant in my blood' at the Last Supper (Luke 22:20), and Hebrews quotes Jer 31:31-34 at length as fulfilled in Christ (Heb 8:8-12).
2387: One of the Latter Prophets in the Hebrew Bible. The Septuagint is about one-eighth shorter than the Hebrew and places the oracles against the nations after Jer 25:13 in a different order; Hebrew fragments from Qumran (e.g. 4QJer-b) support the shorter form, so both may represent ancient editions. On Baruch and the Letter of Jeremiah, see the note on Lamentations.
2389: Poetry (communal and individual laments, mostly acrostic)
2390: Jeremiah. The Septuagint opens with a note that Jeremiah sat weeping and lamented over Jerusalem, and 2 Chr 35:25 records that he composed laments (for Josiah). The Talmud also credits Jeremiah (Baba Bathra 15a).
2391: The book is anonymous in Hebrew. Many scholars think it was written by one or more poets who remained in Judah after 586 BC, noting differences in outlook from Jeremiah (e.g. Lam 4:17-20 appears to put hope in Egypt and in the king, which Jeremiah opposed). Others find the traditional link plausible. The five poems may come from different hands.
2393: Survivors of Jerusalem's destruction, in Judah and in exile, who needed language for grief, confession and faint hope.
2394: Jerusalem in ruins after the Babylonian siege and the burning of the temple in 586 BC.
2395: To grieve the destruction of Jerusalem honestly, to confess that it was the LORD's just judgment, and to cling to his steadfast love and faithfulness in the darkness.
2398: God's steadfast love and new mercies
2401: The city as a desolate widow
2403: The man who has seen affliction
2409: Lamentations stands at the lowest point of Israel's story, after the covenant curses of Deut 28 have fallen, and shows how faith can still pray in the ruins. Jesus' own weeping over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41-44) and the New Testament hope of a renewed city draw on the same grief and hope.
2410: Its Hebrew title *Eikhah* ('How!') is its first word. In the Hebrew Bible it is among the five Megillot in the Writings and is read on Tisha B'Av, the fast commemorating the temple's destruction; Christian Bibles, following the Septuagint, place it after Jeremiah. In Catholic and Orthodox Bibles it is followed by the deuterocanonical *Baruch*, attributed to Jeremiah's scribe, which includes a confession, a wisdom poem and words of comfort to Jerusalem. The *Letter of Jeremiah*, a polemic against idols, is printed as Baruch 6 in Catholic Bibles and as a separate book in Orthodox Bibles. Protestant Bibles that print them place them among the Apocrypha.
2413: Ezekiel son of Buzi, a priest taken to Babylon with King Jehoiachin in 597 BC, who received his visions by the Chebar canal (Ezek 1:1-3). The book is mostly written in the first person and is precisely dated. The Talmud says the 'Men of the Great Assembly' wrote it down (Baba Bathra 15a).
2414: Most scholars accept that the bulk of the book goes back to Ezekiel, with expansion and arrangement by his disciples (Walther Zimmerli's 'school of Ezekiel'). Earlier critics such as Gustav Hölscher (1924) attributed only a small portion of poetry to the prophet; Moshe Greenberg's 'holistic' reading defended the book's coherence. The temple vision (Ezek 40-48) is often seen as containing later priestly elaboration.
2417: Judean exiles in Babylon who thought Jerusalem could not fall, and later, after it fell, who thought they had no future.
2418: Tel-abib by the Chebar canal in Babylonia, between the first deportation (597 BC) and the 27th year of Jehoiachin's exile (571 BC, Ezek 29:17).
2419: To vindicate God's holiness by showing that Jerusalem's fall was just, as the glory of the LORD departed from a defiled temple, and then to promise a new heart, a new spirit, a Davidic shepherd, national resurrection and a renewed temple where 'the LORD is there'.
2420: The glory and holiness of God
2421: 'They shall know that I am the LORD'
2426: Vision of God's glory and Ezekiel's call
2431: Death of Ezekiel's wife; siege begins
2433: The watchman; news of Jerusalem's fall
2435: Valley of dry bones; two sticks joined
2437: Vision of the new temple and land
2440: River of life and the land divided
2441: Ezekiel explains the exile as the departure of God's glory and promises its return in a renewed people and temple. Jesus presents himself as the good shepherd of Ezek 34 (John 10:11), the gift of the Spirit fulfils the promise of a new heart, and Revelation's river of life and holy city draw directly on Ezek 47-48 (Rev 22:1-2).
2442: One of the Latter Prophets in the Hebrew Bible. The Talmud (Shabbat 13b) records that its acceptance was questioned because some of its temple regulations seemed to conflict with the Torah, until Hananiah ben Hezekiah worked out a reconciliation; rabbinic tradition also restricted public reading of its opening chariot vision.
2445: Daniel, a Judean exile taken to Babylon in 605 BC who served under Babylonian and Persian kings until at least the third year of Cyrus (Dan 1:21; Dan 10:1); the visions are written in the first person (Dan 7:2; Dan 8:1). Jesus refers to 'Daniel the prophet' (Matt 24:15). Defenders of a 6th-century date point to the book's place among the Qumran scrolls (with copies dating from the late 2nd century BC), its knowledge of Babylonian figures such as Belshazzar (once doubted, later confirmed by cuneiform texts), and to predictive prophecy as a real possibility.
2446: Most critical scholars date the final book to 167–164 BC, during the persecution of Jews by the Seleucid king Antiochus IV Epiphanes, an argument first made by the Neoplatonist Porphyry (3rd c. AD). They note that the vision of Dan 11 describes Hellenistic history in increasing detail up to Antiochus' desecration of the temple (Dan 11:31) but does not match the circumstances of his death (Dan 11:40-45), suggesting composition just before 164 BC. Many hold that the court stories of Dan 1-6 are older traditions from the Persian or early Hellenistic period, joined to the visions of Dan 7-12 to encourage the persecuted.
2449: Jews living under pagan empires, whether exiles in Babylon (traditional view) or faithful Jews persecuted under Antiochus IV (critical view), called to remain faithful and trust God's coming kingdom.
2450: The Babylonian court of Nebuchadnezzar and Belshazzar and the Persian court of Darius the Mede and Cyrus, from 605 BC to about 536 BC; the visions look forward through Persian and Greek empires to the end.
2451: To show that the God of Israel rules over the kingdoms of the world, gives them to whom he wills and will finally establish an everlasting kingdom; and to encourage faithful conduct and endurance under pressure, with hope of resurrection.
2454: The kingdom of God and the Son of Man
2457: Prologue: faithful exiles at the king's table (Hebrew)
2458: God rules the kingdoms of men (Aramaic section)
2464: Four beasts and the Son of Man
2467: Daniel's prayer and the seventy weeks
2468: Final vision: kings of north and south; resurrection
2469: Daniel widens the biblical story to the scale of world empires and announces that God's kingdom will replace them all. Jesus' favourite self-designation, 'the Son of Man', and his claim to come 'with the clouds of heaven' (Mark 14:62) draw on Dan 7, and Revelation reuses Daniel's imagery extensively.
2470: The book is bilingual: Dan 1:1-2:4 and Dan 8-12 are in Hebrew, Dan 2:4-7:28 in Aramaic. In the Hebrew Bible Daniel is placed among the Writings rather than the Prophets; Christian Bibles, following the Septuagint, place it with the major prophets. Greek Daniel contains additions that are canonical in Catholic (deuterocanonical) and Orthodox Bibles: the *Prayer of Azariah* and the *Song of the Three Young Men* (inserted in Dan 3 after Dan 3:23), *Susanna* (Daniel rescues a falsely accused woman; chapter 13 in Catholic Bibles) and *Bel and the Dragon* (Daniel exposes idol worship; chapter 14). Protestant Bibles that print them place them among the Apocrypha. The church adopted the Greek version attributed to Theodotion in place of the Old Greek translation.
2472: Prophecy (symbolic marriage narrative and poetic oracles)
2473: Hosea son of Beeri, a prophet to the northern kingdom of Israel in the reigns of Jeroboam II of Israel and Uzziah through Hezekiah of Judah (Hos 1:1).
2474: Most scholars accept that the oracles largely go back to Hosea in the northern kingdom, preserved after Samaria's fall by refugees in Judah, who added Judean references and some hopeful passages. The extent of this Judean editing is debated. The Hebrew text is notoriously difficult, possibly reflecting a northern dialect.
2475: Start of ministry under Jeroboam II
2476: Judean edition after the fall of Samaria
2477: The northern kingdom of Israel (often called Ephraim) in its final prosperous and then chaotic decades before Assyria destroyed it.
2478: Israel from the late reign of Jeroboam II (died c. 753 BC) through a series of coups and assassinations to the eve of the fall of Samaria in 722 BC.
2479: To expose Israel's spiritual adultery in Baal worship, political alliances and empty ritual, to announce judgment, and to reveal God's unrelenting covenant love that will woo his people back.
2480: Covenant as marriage; idolatry as adultery
2489: Charges against Israel: no knowledge of God
2490: God's love for Israel his son; judgment and grief
2491: Call to return and promise of healing
2492: Hosea pictures the whole covenant story as a marriage betrayed and restored, a theme that runs through Scripture to the marriage of the Lamb in Revelation. Jesus quotes Hos 6:6 ('I desired mercy, and not sacrifice') twice (Matt 9:13; Matt 12:7), Matthew applies 'out of Egypt have I called my son' to Jesus (Matt 2:15), and Paul uses Hosea's renamed children for the inclusion of Gentiles (Rom 9:25-26).
2493: Hosea opens the Book of the Twelve (the Minor Prophets), counted as a single book in the Hebrew Bible and already known as 'the twelve prophets' by Ben Sira (c. 180 BC). The Septuagint orders the first six differently: Hosea, Amos, Micah, Joel, Obadiah, Jonah. The Hebrew text is divided into chapters slightly differently (English Hos 1:10-2:1 and Hos 11:12 fall in neighbouring chapters).
2496: Joel son of Pethuel (Joel 1:1), about whom nothing else is known. Some traditional scholars place him early, in the minority of King Joash (c. 835 BC), since the book names no king and mentions enemies such as Philistines and Edom.
2497: Many scholars date the book to the Persian period (c. 400 BC), noting the absence of a king, the prominence of priests and elders, the mention of Greeks as slave traders (Joel 3:6), a standing city wall (Joel 2:9) and frequent quotation of other prophets. Others propose a late pre-exilic date. Some scholars argue that the book's second half was added to an original locust lament, while others defend its unity.
2501: The people of Judah and Jerusalem, especially priests and elders, in a time of devastating locust plague and drought.
2502: Judah and Jerusalem with an active temple, after or during a catastrophic locust invasion.
2503: To interpret the locust plague as a warning of the coming Day of the LORD, to call the people to wholehearted repentance, and to promise restoration of the land, the outpouring of God's Spirit on all people and judgment on the nations.
2505: Return to God with all the heart
2507: The Spirit poured out on all flesh
2508: Judgment of the nations and security for Zion
2509: Locust plague and call to lament
2510: The LORD's answer: restoration and the Spirit
2512: Judgment of the nations and blessing for Judah
2513: Joel looks beyond judgment to a day when God's Spirit will rest not only on prophets and kings but on all his people. Peter's sermon at Pentecost declares that this promise is fulfilled (Acts 2:16-21), and Paul cites Joel's 'whosoever shall call on the name of the LORD shall be delivered' as including Jew and Gentile alike (Rom 10:13).
2514: Second book of the Twelve in the Hebrew order. Hebrew Bibles divide Joel into four chapters: English Joel 2:28-32 is Hebrew 3:1-5, and English Joel 3 is Hebrew 4.
2516: Prophecy (oracles, visions and a short narrative)
2517: Amos, a herdsman and dresser of sycamore figs from Tekoa in Judah, called to prophesy against the northern kingdom (Amos 1:1; Amos 7:14-15). He is often called the first of the 'writing prophets'.
